question: Why can a far-away server feel slow even if its code is fast?
options: The server has to send a bigger page when it is far away
Each round trip, including those needed to open the connection, takes longer when the signal travels farther
A far-away server always has a slower CPU
DNS has to be looked up again for every image on the page
explanation: Opening a connection needs one to three round trips before any page data moves, and every round trip takes at least the time the signal needs to cross the distance. The page size and the CPU do not depend on where the server is, and DNS answers are cached.

question: A page takes 2 seconds. The network round trip is 40 ms, and the database query takes 1.6 seconds. What is the best first step?
options: Move the server closer to the users
Make the database query faster, for example with an index or a cache
explanation: The query is 1.6 of the 2 seconds, so improving it helps most. Moving the server or using TLS 1.3 saves at most a few round trips of 40 ms. A second web server does not make one query faster.

question: Estimate: 2 million users each make 15 requests a day. About how many requests per second on average? (Use 1 day ≈ 10⁵ seconds.)
explanation: Step 1, requests per day: 2 million users is 2 × 10⁶, and 2 × 10⁶ × 15 = 30 × 10⁶ = 3 × 10⁷ requests a day. Step 2, per second: one day is 86,400 seconds, rounded to 10⁵, so 3 × 10⁷ ÷ 10⁵ = 3 × 10² = about 300 requests per second. (With the exact 86,400 seconds it is about 347; the rounding keeps the right size.) Peak traffic can be several times the average.
